newsitem.title: MOLDOVA: Moldovan president takes first round election lead.
newsitem.headline: Moldovan president takes first round election lead.

text.p: President Mircea Snegur took a commanding lead in the first round of Moldova's presidential election, but both he and runner-up Petru Lucinschi said on Monday they were confident of victory in the second round.
Snegur, speaking on national radio after early results came out, described his victory as a rebuff to conservatives.
"The...votes cast for me are a resolute rebuff to all revanchist and conservative forces of the left," he said.
"We have two more weeks -- enough time to mobilise forces and win in the second round."

Lucinschi, chairman of parliament in the tiny former Soviet republic, told a news conference he remained confident of final victory. "Experience of other states shows that those second after the first round often become first after a run-off."
The run-off will be on December 1.

The Central Electoral Commission said preliminary results showed that the centre-right Snegur, who was backed by several nationalist groups, had won 39 percent of Sunday's vote, well short of the 50 percent needed to win in one round.
Lucinschi, who presents himself as a moderate centrist, won 28 percent.

Seven other contenders, including Prime Minister Andrei Sangheli, were far behind. Sangheli got just nine percent of the vote, one point behind Communist Party leader Vladimir Voronin. Nationalist Valeriu Matei received nine percent.
One of Lucinschi's aides said Lucinschi expected the backing of defeated candidates Sangheli and Voronin. "In this case, our victory is more than probable," Vladimir Solonari told Reuters.
Independent experts predicted a close race in the run-off.

"If you use primitive arithmetic, Lucinschi's chances are better," political expert Oazu Nantoi told Reuters. "But his possible allies differ too much, so it will be a very close fight, whose outcome is hard to predict."
Sunday's poll was the first multi-candidate presidential election in landlocked Moldova, which is sandwiched between Ukraine and Romania.

Moldovan nationalists have long sought a union with Romania, which shares a common language and culture. Snegur advocates stronger ties with Bucharest, but he has also said that Moldova should remain independent.
The campaigns of Snegur and Lucinschi were contrasting.

Snegur, 56, was aggressive and populist, criss-crossing the impoverished country of 4.3 million with a simple message: "I feel for you and, if you give me four more years and more powers, I'll help you."
He has vowed to amend the constitution, probably through a referendum, to turn Moldova into a presidential republic and to force out the government and parliament.

Lucinschi, a 56-year-old bespectacled intellectual, has accused Snegur of acting unconstitutionally and leading Moldova towards confrontation. He ran as an independent and was backed by a number of leftist parties.

Lucinschi, the former leader of the Communist Party in Soviet Moldova, also said he was best placed to settle the conflict with separatists in Dnestr, a predominantly Slav region in the east of the wedge-shaped country which fears that they could lose out if Moldova moved closer to Romania.
Many voters also believed Lucinschi would help develop ties with Russia, Moldova's main market and energy supplier.
